lessons.title: Body Parts and Health Vocabulary
lessons.body:
Start by learning the Swahili words for the body parts you will need most in a health emergency. The head is kichwa, and the brain is ubongo. Your eyes are macho, ears masikio, nose pua, and mouth mdomo. The neck is shingo, chest kifua, stomach tumbo, and back mgongo. Arms are mikono, hands viganja, fingers vidole, legs miguu, and feet nyayo. For internal parts, the heart is moyo, lungs mapafu, liver ini, and kidneys figo. Practice pointing to each part and saying the word aloud until you can do it without looking.

Next, learn words for common health states. Being healthy is kuwa na afya. Pain is maumivu, and you can say I have pain in my head: Nina maumivu ya kichwa. Fever is homa, cough kikohozi, and cold baridi. A wound is jeraha, and bleeding is kutokwa na damu. Vomiting is kutapika, diarrhea kuhara, and dizziness kizunguzungu. If you feel weak, say nina udhaifu. For allergies, use mzio. These words will help you describe what is wrong quickly.

In many African clinics, you will be asked to fill out a form or tell the receptionist your problem. Knowing these words saves time. For example, at a health center in Kenya or Tanzania, you might hear: Umeumwa wapi? (Where does it hurt?) You can reply: Naumwa hapa (It hurts here) and point. If you need a doctor, say Nahitaji daktari. For a nurse, nahitaji muuguzi. If you are pregnant, mimba is the word, and labor is uchungu wa kuzaa. For children, mtoto wangu ni mgonjwa means my child is sick.

Practice with a friend: name each body part in Swahili, then say a simple sentence like Nina maumivu ya tumbo (I have stomach pain). Use a mirror to point to your own body. Make flashcards with the Swahili word on one side and the English on the other. Review daily for one week. You will be surprised how quickly you can communicate in a clinic or hospital. Remember, clear communication can save a life.

lessons.title: Describing Symptoms
lessons.body:
When you are sick, you need to tell a health worker exactly what you feel. Start with the main symptom. For pain, say Nina maumivu ya [body part]. For example, Nina maumivu ya kichwa (I have a headache). If the pain is sharp, say maumivu makali; if it is dull, maumivu ya kawaida. For fever, say Nina homa. To describe how long, use siku (days): Nina homa kwa siku tatu (I have had fever for three days). For cough, Nina kikohozi. If you are coughing blood, say Ninakohoa damu. That is serious.

For stomach problems: Nina maumivu ya tumbo (stomach ache), Ninatapika (I am vomiting), Ninahara (I have diarrhea). If you cannot keep food down, say Siwezi kula. For dizziness, Nina kizunguzungu. For difficulty breathing, Nina shida kupumua. For a rash, Nina vipele. For swelling, Nina uvimbe. If you have a wound, say Nina jeraha, and if it is bleeding, Nina jeraha linalotokwa na damu. For a headache with fever, say Nina maumivu ya kichwa na homa.

In African clinics, you may be asked: Unajisikiaje? (How do you feel?) Or: Unaumwa wapi? (Where does it hurt?) Answer clearly. If you have a chronic condition like diabetes (kisukari) or high blood pressure (shinikizo la damu), say Nina kisukari or Nina shinikizo la damu. For malaria, say Nina malaria. If you are pregnant, say Nina mimba. For a child, say Mtoto wangu ana homa (My child has a fever).

Use numbers: temperature is joto la mwili. A normal temperature is around 37Â°C. If you have a thermometer, you can say: Joto langu ni 38.5. For pain scale, 1 to 10: maumivu ni 7 kwa 10. Be honest. If you have been vomiting for two days, say Ninatapika kwa siku mbili. If you have diarrhea more than three times a day, say Ninahara mara nyingi. This helps the nurse decide quickly.

Practice with a partner: one plays the patient, the other the nurse. Use real scenarios: malaria, stomach flu, a cut. Describe the symptom, duration, and severity. Record yourself and listen. In an emergency, you will be ready.

lessons.title: At the Pharmacy
lessons.body:
Pharmacies in Africa are called duka la dawa. When you enter, greet the pharmacist: Habari za asubuhi (Good morning) or Habari za mchana (Good afternoon). Then say: Nahitaji dawa (I need medicine). If you have a prescription, say: Nina hati ya dawa. If not, describe your symptoms: Nina homa na kikohozi (I have fever and cough). The pharmacist may ask: Una umri gani? (How old are you?) or Una miaka mingapi? Answer with your age: Nina miaka 30. For a child, say: Mtoto ana miaka 5.

Common medicines: paracetamol for pain and fever (dawa ya maumivu na homa), antibiotics (dawa ya bakteria), antimalarials (dawa ya malaria), and ORS (oral rehydration salts) for diarrhea (dawa ya kuhara). If you need a painkiller, say: Nahitaji dawa ya maumivu. For cough syrup, dawa ya kikohozi. For malaria, dawa ya malaria. If you are allergic to penicillin, say: Nina mzio wa penicillin. Always ask: Hii ni dawa gani? (What is this medicine?) and Jinsi ya kutumia? (How to use it?). The pharmacist might say: Kunywa kidonge kimoja mara mbili kwa siku (Take one pill twice a day). Or: Paka mafuta (Apply ointment).

Payment: Ask Bei gani? (How much?) or Ni shilingi ngapi? In Kenya, use shilingi; in Tanzania, shilingi; in Uganda, shilingi. If you have insurance, say: Nina bima. If you need a receipt, say: Naomba risiti. If the medicine is too expensive, say: Ni ghali sana. Je, una nafuu? (It's too expensive. Do you have a cheaper one?)

Always check the expiry date: Tarehe ya mwisho. Do not buy expired drugs. Ask for generic alternatives: Dawa ya jina la kawaida. For children, ask for syrup: dawa ya maji. For adults, tablets: vidonge. If you cannot read the label, ask the pharmacist to explain again: Tafadhali eleza tena. Repeat back the instructions to be sure. For example: Kunywa kidonge kimoja asubuhi na jioni? The pharmacist will confirm. Keep your medicines in a cool, dry place. Never share antibiotics. If symptoms persist after three days, return to the pharmacy or go to a clinic.

lessons.title: Emergency Situations
lessons.body:
In an emergency, every second counts. Learn these Swahili phrases: Msada! (Help!) or Saidieni! (Help me!). If someone is unconscious, say: Amepoteza fahamu. If they are not breathing, say: Hapumui. If they are bleeding heavily, say: Anatokwa na damu nyingi. For a broken bone, say: Amevunjika mfupa. For a burn, say: Ameungua. For a snake bite, say: Ameng'atwa na nyoka. For a heart attack, say: Ana shida ya moyo. For a stroke, say: Ana shida ya kiharusi.

Call for help: In Kenya, dial 999 or 112 for ambulance. In Tanzania, 112. In Uganda, 999 or 112. Say: Nahitaji gari la wagonjwa (I need an ambulance). Give your location: Tuko [place name]. For example: Tuko Kenyatta Hospital. If you are in a remote area, say: Tuko kijijini. If you have a phone, use it. If not, shout for help and send someone to the nearest health center.

First aid steps: For bleeding, press firmly on the wound with a clean cloth. Say: Shikilia hapa kwa nguvu. For burns, cool with clean water for 10 minutes. Say: Weka maji baridi. For a fracture, do not move the person. Say: Usimsogeze. For choking, give back blows. Say: Piga mgongoni. For fainting, lay the person flat and raise legs. Say: Lalisha na inua miguu. For seizures, protect the head and do not put anything in the mouth. Say: Linda kichwa, usiweke kitu mdomoni.

In a road accident, say: Ajali! (Accident!). If there is fire, say: Moto! If someone is drowning, say: Anazama. If you are in a crowd, ask for space: Nipisheni! (Let me through!). If you need to move someone, say: Tusaidie kumsogeza. Always keep a first aid kit (sanduku la huduma ya kwanza) with bandages, antiseptic, gloves, and ORS. Know the nearest hospital: hospitali ya karibu. Practice these phrases until they are automatic. In an emergency, you will not have time to think.

lessons.title: Asking for Help
lessons.body:
Asking for help in Swahili is simple but must be clear. The most common phrase is: Naomba msaada (I ask for help). Or simply: Msaada! (Help!). If you need a doctor, say: Naomba daktari. For a nurse: Naomba muuguzi. For an ambulance: Naomba gari la wagonjwa. If you are lost, say: Nimepotea. If you are in danger, say: Nina hatari. If you are sick, say: Mimi ni mgonjwa. If someone else is sick, say: Yeye ni mgonjwa.

When you ask for help, be specific. Instead of just saying Msaada, say: Naomba msaada wa daktari (I need a doctor's help). Or: Naomba msaada wa haraka (I need urgent help). If you need directions to a hospital, say: Hospitali iko wapi? (Where is the hospital?). If you need a pharmacy, say: Duka la dawa liko wapi? If you need a police station, say: Kituo cha polisi kiko wapi? If you need a phone, say: Naomba simu. If you need money for transport, say: Naomba nauli.

In African communities, people are often willing to help. But you must ask politely. Use tafadhali (please) and asante (thank you). For example: Tafadhali, nisaidie (Please help me). If you are asking a group, say: Tafadhalini, nisaidieni. If you are asking a respected elder, say: Naomba msaada wako. If you are in a market or bus station, ask the vendor or conductor: Naomba msaada wako. They may point you to a clinic or call someone.

If you are a victim of crime, say: Nimeibiwa (I have been robbed). Nimevamiwa (I have been attacked). Call the police: Polisi! If you are in a domestic violence situation, say: Naomba msaada, nina shida nyumbani. If you need a shelter, say: Naomba mahali pa kulala. If you need food, say: Naomba chakula. If you need water, say: Naomba maji. Do not be ashamed to ask. In Swahili culture, helping others is part of jamii (community). Practice these phrases with a friend. Role-play: you are lost in a new city, you are sick, you are in an accident. The more you practice, the more confident you will be.

lessons.title: Making a Doctor's Appointment
lessons.body:
To make an appointment in Swahili, start by calling or visiting the clinic. Say: Naomba kuonana na daktari (I would like to see a doctor). Or: Naweza kupata miadi? (Can I get an appointment?). The receptionist may ask: Una shida gani? (What is your problem?) or Unataka kuonana na nani? (Who do you want to see?). Answer clearly: Nina maumivu ya tumbo (I have stomach pain). Or: Nahitaji uchunguzi (I need a check-up).

Give your name: Jina langu ni [your name]. Give your phone number: Namba yangu ya simu ni [number]. Ask for a specific date and time: Je, naweza kuja kesho? (Can I come tomorrow?) Or: Je, kuna nafasi leo? (Is there space today?). If you need an urgent appointment, say: Ni dharura (It's an emergency). If you can wait, say: Ni miadi ya kawaida (It's a regular appointment). The receptionist might say: Kuja kesho saa tatu asubuhi (Come tomorrow at 9 AM). Repeat back to confirm: Kesho saa tatu asubuhi, sawa? (Tomorrow at 9 AM, okay?).

If you need to cancel or reschedule, call and say: Naomba kufuta miadi yangu (I would like to cancel my appointment). Or: Naomba kubadilisha miadi (I would like to change my appointment). If you are running late, call and say: Nimechelewa, nitafika baada ya dakika 15 (I am late, I will arrive in 15 minutes). If you cannot come, say: Siwezi kufika leo. If you need a home visit, ask: Je, daktari anaweza kuja nyumbani? (Can the doctor come to my home?).

When you arrive for your appointment, greet: Habari za asubuhi. Then say: Nina miadi na daktari [name]. If you are new, say: Mimi ni mgonjwa mpya (I am a new patient). If you are returning, say: Mimi ni mgonjwa wa kurudi (I am a returning patient). Bring your health card: kadi ya afya. If you have insurance, bring your insurance card: kadi ya bima. If you need a translator, ask: Naomba mtafsiri. If you need a female doctor, say: Naomba daktari wa kike. If you need a male doctor, say: Naomba daktari wa kiume. After the appointment, ask: Ni dawa gani? (What medicine?) and: Nifanye nini nyumbani? (What should I do at home?). Write down the instructions. If you don't understand, say: Tafadhali rudia (Please repeat). Always confirm the next appointment: Miadi ijayo ni lini? (When is the next appointment?).

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Health & Emergency Swahili for African Agribusiness

In agribusiness, your most valuable asset is the people who plant, harvest, process, and sell. When a worker, supplier, or customer falls ill or an accident happens on the farm, at a market stall, or on a long-distance transport route, the ability to communicate clearly in Swahili can mean the difference between a minor disruption and a major loss. This Practical Reference lesson equips you with the exact phrases, vocabulary, and cultural protocols you need to handle health and emergency situations across East and Central Africa â from a rural clinic in Tanzania to a pharmacy in Nairobi's Eastleigh, from a produce market in Kampala to a border post in Goma.

Swahili (Kiswahili) is the lingua franca of the East African Community â Tanzania, Kenya, Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi, South Sudan, and the DRC â a combined market of over 300 million people and the backbone of Africa's cross-border agricultural trade. Whether you manage a coffee cooperative in Mbeya, a horticultural export operation near Arusha, or a livestock trading route through Mwanza, you will interact with health systems in Swahili. This lesson is business-first: every phrase is chosen because it protects productivity, reduces liability, and strengthens the trust that keeps supply chains running.

Core Vocabulary: Body Parts and Health Terms

Before you can describe a symptom, you need the building blocks. The table below covers the body parts and health terms most relevant to agribusiness operations â injuries from tools, heat exhaustion in the field, and common illnesses that affect workforce availability.

Table 1: Essential Body Parts and Health Vocabulary (SwahiliâEnglish)
Swahili English Agribusiness Context
KichwaHeadHeat stroke, headache from sun exposure
MachoEyesChemical splash from pesticides
MasikioEarsNoise from machinery
MdomoMouthIngestion of contaminated water
KooThroatSore throat, difficulty swallowing
KifuaChestRespiratory issues from dust
MoyoHeartCardiac emergencies
TumboStomachFood poisoning, cholera
MgongoBackLifting injuries from sacks
MikonoArms/HandsCuts, fractures from tools
VidoleFingersMachete and machine injuries
MiguuLegsSnake bites, falls
MguuFootPuncture wounds, infections
DamuBloodBleeding control
HomaFeverMalaria, typhoid
MaumivuPainGeneral symptom descriptor
UgonjwaIllness/DiseaseDiagnosis communication
DawaMedicinePharmacy and treatment
DaktariDoctorMedical professional
HospitaliHospitalFacility navigation
KlinikiClinicLocal health facility
Duka la dawaPharmacyMedicine purchase
AjaliAccidentEmergency reporting
DharuraEmergencyUrgent situations
MsaadaHelpRequesting assistance
PumzikaRestWorker recovery instruction
ChanjoVaccinationWorkforce health compliance
UchunguziExamination/TestDiagnostic procedures

Source: Compiled from TUKI, Kamusi ya Kiswahili Sanifu (2013); Peace Corps Tanzania, Kiswahili Language Manual (2019); and WHO Africa Region, Community Health Worker Training Materials â East Africa (2021).

Describing Symptoms: The Business Case for Clarity

When a worker says "Naumwa" (I am sick), you have a productivity problem. When they say "Naumwa na tumbo, nina kuhara, na nimekosa nguvu" (I have stomach pain, diarrhea, and weakness), you have actionable information. Clear symptom description reduces misdiagnosis, prevents the spread of infectious disease through your workforce, and ensures the right treatment is sought the first time â saving time, money, and health.

Use the pattern Naumwa na [body part] for localized pain, and Nina [symptom] for conditions. For duration, add kwa siku [number] (for [number] days). For severity, use kidogo (a little), sana (very much), or siwezi kuvumilia (I cannot bear it).

Table 2: Symptom Description Patterns and Emergency Phrases
Swahili Phrase English Meaning When to Use
Naumwa na kichwa sanaI have a severe headacheHeat stroke, malaria, dehydration
Nina homa na ninatetemekaI have a fever and I am shiveringMalaria, typhoid, infection
Nina kuhara na kutapikaI have diarrhea and vomitingCholera, food poisoning
Siwezi kupumua vizuriI cannot breathe wellRespiratory emergency, allergic reaction
Nina damu nyingiI am bleeding heavilyCut, accident, injury
Nimeumia mguu wanguI hurt my legFall, machinery accident
Nina maumivu ya kifuaI have chest painCardiac, respiratory
Nina kichefuchefuI feel nauseousPesticide exposure, illness
Nimechoka sana na nina kizunguzunguI am very tired and dizzyHeat exhaustion, anemia
Nina ugonjwa wa ngoziI have a skin diseaseFungal infection, contact dermatitis
Naumwa na jinoI have a toothacheDental emergency
Nina maumivu ya mgongoI have back painLifting injury, chronic condition
Nimeumia kwa motoI am burnedFire, chemical burn
Nimeumia kwa chumaI am cut by metalMachete, machinery
Nimegusa sumuI touched poison/pesticideChemical exposure
Ninahitaji msaada harakaI need help quicklyAny emergency
Nipeleke hospitaliniTake me to the hospitalUrgent transport request
Ita daktari / Ita gari la hospitaliCall a doctor / Call an ambulanceEmergency escalation

Source: Compiled from Peace Corps Tanzania, Kiswahili Language Manual (2019); WHO Africa Region, Community Health Worker Training Materials (2021); and Kenya Ministry of Health, Emergency Care Training Manual (2020).

At the Pharmacy: Duka la Dawa

In most East African agribusiness communities, the pharmacy is the first point of care. Pharmacists and pharmacy attendants in Tanzania, Kenya, and Uganda are often the most accessible health professionals. Knowing how to describe your needs clearly â and understanding what you are being sold â protects your workers and your business from counterfeit or inappropriate medication.

Key phrases: Nina dawa ya [ugonjwa]? (Do you have medicine for [illness]?) â¢ Bei gani? (What is the price?) â¢ Nitumie dawa hii vipi? (How do I take this medicine?) â¢ Kwa siku ngapi? (For how many days?) â¢ Nina mzio wa dawa hii (I am allergic to this medicine) â¢ Naomba risiti (I need a receipt â essential for business expense records and insurance claims).

Always ask for the generic name (jina la kawaida) and check the expiry date (tarehe ya kumalizika). In agribusiness, where you may be purchasing medicine for multiple workers, buy from registered pharmacies (duka la dawa lililosajiliwa) and keep records. Counterfeit antimalarials and antibiotics are a documented problem across the region; WHO estimates that 1 in 10 medical products in low- and middle-income countries is substandard or falsified.

â ï¸ RED SAFETY WARNING â DHARURA YA AFYA

If a worker shows any of the following signs, treat it as a life-threatening emergency. Do not wait for a scheduled appointment. Call for emergency transport immediately and use these phrases:

  • Siwezi kupumua â Cannot breathe (respiratory failure, severe allergic reaction)
  • Nina maumivu ya kifua na jasho baridi â Chest pain with cold sweat (possible heart attack)
  • Nina damu nyingi na siwezi kusimama â Heavy bleeding and cannot stand (hemorrhage)
  • Nimegusa sumu ya kilimo â Touched agricultural pesticide (organophosphate poisoning)
  • Nina homa kali na shingo ngumu â High fever with stiff neck (possible meningitis)
  • Amepoteza fahamu â He/she has lost consciousness

Emergency numbers: Kenya 999 / 112 â¢ Tanzania 112 / 114 â¢ Uganda 999 / 112 â¢ Rwanda 112 â¢ DRC 112. Save these in every company phone. For pesticide poisoning, bring the product label or container to the hospital â the active ingredient determines the antidote.

Emergency Situations and Asking for Help

Farm accidents are common and often preventable: machete cuts, tractor rollovers, snake bites, chemical exposure, falls from storage structures, and heat stroke. In an emergency, seconds matter. Your team should know three things: how to call for help, how to describe the emergency, and how to get the patient to care.

Essential emergency phrases: Msaada! Ajali imetokea! (Help! An accident has happened!) â¢ Mtu ameumia (Someone is injured) â¢ Mtu ameanguka (Someone has fallen) â¢ Mtu amezimia (Someone has fainted) â¢ Mtu amepigwa na nyoka (Someone has been bitten by a snake) â¢ Mtu amegusa sumu (Someone has touched poison) â¢ Mtu ameungua (Someone is burned) â¢ Haraka! Haraka! (Quickly! Quickly!)

When calling for help, state: your location (mahali), what happened (nini kilitokea), how many people are affected (watu wangapi), and what help you need (msaada gani). If you are in a remote area, give a landmark â karibu na shamba la kahawa (near the coffee farm), kando ya barabara ya Mwanza (beside the Mwanza road).

Making a Doctor's Appointment

For non-emergency care â routine check-ups, follow-up visits, occupational health assessments, and vaccination campaigns â you will need to schedule appointments. In agribusiness, this matters for workforce health compliance, insurance requirements, and maintaining productivity.

Phrases: Ningependa kuonana na daktari (I would like to see a doctor) â¢ Naweza kupata miadi?

quiz.q: What is the Swahili word for 'head'?
quiz.explanation: Kichwa means head, while moyo is heart, tumbo is stomach, and mkono is arm/hand.

quiz.q: How do you say 'I have a headache' in Swahili?
quiz.explanation: Nina maumivu ya kichwa translates to 'I have pain of the head', i.e., a headache.

quiz.q: What is the Swahili word for 'fever'?
quiz.explanation: Homa means fever, while kikohozi is cough, maumivu is pain, and jeraha is wound.

quiz.q: Which phrase means 'I need a doctor'?
quiz.explanation: Nahitaji daktari means 'I need a doctor', while muuguzi is nurse and dawa is medicine.

quiz.q: What does 'Ninatapika' mean?
quiz.explanation: Ninatapika comes from kutapika, meaning 'to vomit'.

quiz.q: How do you say 'I have diarrhea' in Swahili?
quiz.explanation: Ninahara means 'I have diarrhea', from kuhara.

quiz.q: What is the Swahili word for 'pharmacy'?
quiz.explanation: Duka la dawa literally means 'shop of medicine', i.e., pharmacy.

quiz.q: If you need painkillers, what do you ask for?
quiz.explanation: Dawa ya maumivu means 'medicine for pain', i.e., painkillers.

quiz.q: How do you say 'I am allergic to penicillin'?
quiz.explanation: Nina mzio wa penicillin means 'I have an allergy to penicillin'.

quiz.q: What does 'Bei gani?' mean?
quiz.explanation: Bei gani? is a common way to ask 'How much?' or 'What is the price?'

quiz.q: Which phrase means 'Help!' in Swahili?
quiz.explanation: Msaada! means 'Help!' and is used in emergencies.

quiz.q: How do you say 'He is not breathing'?
quiz.explanation: Hapumui means 'he/she is not breathing', from kupumua (to breathe).

quiz.q: What number do you dial for an ambulance in Kenya?
quiz.explanation: In Kenya, both 999 and 112 are emergency numbers for ambulance and police.

quiz.q: What is the Swahili word for 'accident'?
quiz.explanation: Ajali means accident, while moto is fire, dharura is emergency, and hatari is danger.

quiz.q: How do you say 'I need urgent help'?
quiz.explanation: Naomba msaada wa haraka means 'I need urgent help'.

quiz.q: What does 'Nimepotea' mean?
quiz.explanation: Nimepotea means 'I have gotten lost' or 'I am lost'.

quiz.q: How do you ask 'Where is the hospital?'
options: B) Duka la dawa liko wapi?
C) Kituo cha polisi kiko wapi?
quiz.explanation: Hospitali iko wapi? means 'Where is the hospital?'

quiz.q: What is the polite way to say 'Please help me' to one person?
quiz.explanation: Tafadhali nisaidie is singular polite; tafadhalini nisaidieni is plural.

quiz.q: How do you say 'I would like to see a doctor'?
quiz.explanation: Naomba kuonana na daktari means 'I ask to see a doctor'.

quiz.q: What does 'Ni dharura' mean?
options: B) It is a regular appointment
quiz.explanation: Ni dharura means 'It is an emergency'.

quiz.q: How do you ask 'Can I come tomorrow?'
quiz.explanation: Kesho means tomorrow, so 'Je, naweza kuja kesho?' means 'Can I come tomorrow?'

quiz.q: What is the Swahili word for 'appointment'?
quiz.explanation: Miadi means appointment, while dawa is medicine, hospitali is hospital, and daktari is doctor.

quiz.q: How do you say 'I have a stomach ache'?
quiz.explanation: Tumbo means stomach, so 'Nina maumivu ya tumbo' means 'I have a stomach ache'.

quiz.q: What does 'Nina kizunguzungu' mean?
quiz.explanation: Kizunguzungu means dizziness, so 'Nina kizunguzungu' means 'I am dizzy'.

quiz.q: How do you say 'I need medicine'?
quiz.explanation: Dawa means medicine, so 'Nahitaji dawa' means 'I need medicine'.

quiz.q: What is the Swahili word for 'wound'?
quiz.explanation: Jeraha means wound, while maumivu is pain, homa is fever, and kikohozi is cough.

quiz.q: How do you say 'Call an ambulance'?
quiz.explanation: Gari la wagonjwa means ambulance, so 'Ita gari la wagonjwa' means 'Call an ambulance'.

quiz.q: What does 'Nina hatari' mean?
quiz.explanation: Hatari means danger, so 'Nina hatari' means 'I am in danger'.

quiz.q: How do you ask 'What is this medicine?'
quiz.explanation: Hii ni dawa gani? means 'What medicine is this?'

quiz.q: What is the Swahili word for 'nurse'?
quiz.explanation: Muuguzi means nurse, while daktari is doctor and mgonjwa is patient.
